questions.q: What failure mode does an FCI protect against, and what is its real single point of failure?
options: It protects against node failure; the shared storage itself is a single point of failure
It protects against storage failure; the node is the single point of failure
It protects against both node and storage failure equally
FCIs have no single point of failure at all
questions.explain: An FCI's nodes share one copy of the data — if that shared storage fails, every node loses access simultaneously.

questions.q: Why does an Availability Group survive a storage failure on the primary replica, when an FCI would not survive its shared storage failing?
options: Each AG replica has its own independent storage, so a failure on one replica's storage doesn't affect another's
AG replicas don't use storage at all
AG automatically repairs failed storage devices
AGs use the exact same shared storage architecture as FCIs
questions.explain: AG replicates at the database level to replicas with independent storage, unlike FCI's single shared copy.

questions.q: What tradeoff does AG bring that a single-instance FCI generally does not require as heavily?
options: More involved edition/licensing considerations, especially with features like readable secondaries
A requirement for shared storage across all replicas
The complete elimination of any licensing costs
A hard limit of exactly one replica
questions.explain: Multiple AG replicas and features like readable secondaries bring licensing/edition considerations that a single FCI instance doesn't need to the same degree.

questions.q: What is the honest real-world pattern this lesson describes for combining FCI and AG?
options: Run an FCI within each site for node protection, then build an AG between FCIs at different sites for storage/site protection
Never use both together under any circumstances
Always replace FCI entirely with AG in every deployment
Use FCI only for test environments and AG only for production
questions.explain: Layering FCI within a site and AG between sites is a deliberate, common design that covers both failure modes.

questions.q: A team's shared SAN fails completely while running a plain FCI with no AG on top. What happens?
options: SQL Server does not successfully fail over — every node loses access to the same shared storage at once
SQL Server automatically fails over to a node with its own independent copy of the data
The FCI switches to an AG configuration automatically
Nothing happens because FCIs don't depend on shared storage
questions.explain: Because an FCI has only one copy of the data on shared storage, a failure of that storage affects every node simultaneously — there's no independent copy to fail over to.
